content: 1. Although genotypic testing may not always yield successful results, it remains a critical consideration in clinical decision-making (BII). 2. Drug-resistance testing is essential when managing cases of suboptimal viral load reduction to guide therapy adjustments (AII). 3. In cases of virologic failure during treatment with an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI)-based regimen, genotypic testing for INSTI resistance should be conducted to determine whether drugs from this class should be included in subsequent regimens (AII). 4. Drug-resistance testing in the context of virologic failure should ideally be performed while the patient is still taking antiretroviral (ARV) drugs or, if not feasible, within four weeks of discontinuing therapy (AII). 5. If more than four weeks have passed since ARV discontinuation, resistance testing may still provide useful information for guiding therapy. However, it is important to recognize that previously selected resistance mutations may not be detected (CIII). 6. Genotypic testing is the preferred method for resistance testing in patients with suboptimal virologic response or virologic failure while on firstor second-line regimens (AII). 7. Adding phenotypic testing to genotypic testing is generally recommended for individuals with known or suspected complex drug-resistance mutation patterns (BIII). 8. Resistance testing for mutations associated with resistance to the fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide is commercially available. 9. Genotypic assays can be performed rapidly, with results typically available within one to two weeks of sample collection. 10. Interpreting genotypic test results requires expertise in understanding the mutations selected by different ARV drugs and the potential for cross-resistance to other drugs conferred by specific mutations. 11. The International AIDS Society-USA (IAS-USA) maintains an updated list of significant resistance-associated mutations in the reverse transcriptase (RT), protease (PR), integrase (IN), and envelope genes. 12. The Stanford University HIV Drug Resistance Database provides valuable guidance for interpreting genotypic resistance test results. 13. Various tools are now available to assist clinicians in interpreting genotypic test results. 14. Clinical trials have demonstrated that consulting with specialists in HIV drug resistance improves virologic outcomes. 15. Clinicians are encouraged to consult specialists to interpret genotypic test results and design optimal new regimens. 16. 17. RT, PR, integrase, and envelope gene sequences derived from patient plasma HIV RNA are inserted into a laboratory clone of HIV or used to generate pseudotyped viruses expressing patient-derived HIV genes of interest. 18. The replication of these viruses at different drug concentrations is monitored by the expression of a reporter gene and compared to the replication of a reference HIV strain. 19. The drug concentration that inhibits viral replication by 50% (IC50) is calculated, and the ratio of the IC50 of test and reference viruses is reported as the fold increase in IC50 (fold resistance). 20. Automated phenotypic assays, which can produce results in two to three weeks, are commercially available but are more expensive than genotypic assays. 21. Interpreting phenotypic assay results is complicated by incomplete information regarding the specific resistance level (fold increase in IC50) associated with drug failure, although clinically significant fold increase cutoffs are now available for some drugs. 22. Consulting with a specialist to interpret phenotypic test results can be beneficial. 23. Limitations of both genotypic and phenotypic assays include the lack of uniform quality assurance testing for all available assays, relatively high costs, and insensitivity to minor viral species. 24. Drug-resistant viruses that constitute less than 10% to 20% of the circulating viral population are unlikely to be detected by commercially available assays. 25. 26. Consequently, the proportion of virus with resistance mutations decreases to below the 10% to 20% detection threshold. 27. For some drugs, this reversion to predominantly wild-type virus can occur within the first four to six weeks after drug discontinuation. 28. Prospective clinical studies have shown that despite plasma reversion, re-initiation of the same ARV agents (or those sharing similar resistance pathways) is usually associated with early drug failure, and the virus present at failure is derived from previously archived resistant virus. 29. Therefore, resistance testing is most valuable when performed before or within four weeks after drug discontinuation (AII). 30. Because resistant virus may persist longer in the plasma of some patients, resistance testing conducted four to six weeks after drug discontinuation may still detect mutations. 31. However, the absence of detectable resistance in such patients must be interpreted cautiously when designing subsequent ARV regimens. 32. Transmission of drug-resistant HIV strains is well-documented and associated with suboptimal virologic response to initial antiretroviral therapy (ART). 33. The risk of acquiring drug-resistant virus is related to the prevalence of drug resistance in HIV-infected individuals engaging in high-risk behaviors within a given community. 34. In high-income countries (e.g., the United States, some European countries, Australia, and Japan), approximately 10% to 17% of ART-naive patients have resistance mutations to at least one ARV drug. 35. Up to 8%, but generally less than 5%, of transmitted viruses exhibit resistance to drugs from more than one class. 36. Transmitted resistant HIV is generally either NRTIor NNRTI-resistant. 37. PI resistance is much less common, and transmitted INSTI resistance is rare. 38. In individuals with acute or recent (early) HIV infection, resistance testing can guide therapy selection to optimize virologic response. 39. Therefore, resistance testing in this situation is recommended (AII). 40. A genotypic assay is preferred for this purpose (AIII). 41. In this setting, treatment initiation should not be delayed pending resistance testing results if the patient is willing and able to begin treatment. 42. Once results are reported, the regimen can be modified if warranted. 43. In the absence of ART, resistant viruses may decline over time to below the detection limit of standard resistance tests. 44. However, when ART is eventually initiated, even low levels of resistant viruses may still increase the risk of treatment failure. 45. Therefore, if ART is deferred, resistance testing should still be performed during acute HIV infection (AIII). 46. In this situation, the genotypic resistance test result may be kept on record until the patient begins ART. 47. Repeat resistance testing at the start of treatment may be considered because a patient may acquire drug-resistant virus (e.g., superinfection) between entry into care and initiation of ART (CIII). 48. Interpretation of drug-resistance testing before ART initiation in patients with chronic HIV infection is less straightforward. 49. The rate at which transmitted resistance-associated mutations revert to wild-type virus has not been completely delineated, but mutations present at the time of HIV transmission are likely to persist longer.
